newsitem.title: BULGARIA: ECONOMIC CRISIS HITS BULGARIAN PRISONS.
newsitem.headline: ECONOMIC CRISIS HITS BULGARIAN PRISONS.

text.p: Bulgaria's severe economic crisis means prisoners languishing in the country's jails are now suffering food shortages as well as the delays endemic in the country's legal system.

Prisons chief Zdravko Traikov said every third prisoner was under investigation or on trial rather than serving a sentence, and there were several attempted suicides and hunger strikes each year as a protest against delays.

"Prisoners understand very well what the situation in the country is and tension comes not so much from malnutrition as from having to stay in prison without a final verdict even for more than a year," Traikov said in an interview.
He told Reuters it was impossible to feed the country's 11,000 prisoners properly and meat could now be served only once in two weeks.
But he denied a newspaper report that the government planned to free 3,000 prisoners because it could not feed them.
January was a difficult month for the prisons management as its funding was enough to buy bread only, other officials said.
Some jails were forced to delay paying staff wages to buy food for the prisoners.
"In 1995, the daily allowances for food per prisoner were worth 50.60 levs, last year they were 52 levs and now we spend more than 250 levs per person each day," Traikov said.
Soaring inflation has melted the lev's buying power since the beginning of the year.

Police said they expected the economic crisis to bring a further crime boom. More than 500,000 of the 8.4-million population is unemployed, monthly wages are worth $10 and pensions are around $3 per month.
Planned judicial reforms have not yet borne fruit and Bulgaria's legal system lacks the staff to deal with a big rise in crime since the end of communist rule in 1989.
One magistrate said he had more than 500 cases on his desk including murders and rapes and he could not pass on each one to the court within the required two month term.
"Delays of sentences are due to sluggishness of the judicial system," Traikov said.

Charges are even still outstanding against former communist leader Todor Zhivkov, who is still under house arrest although the Sofia civil prosecutor last month freed him in connection with embezzlement charges.

The 85-year-old Zhivkov, who ruled Bulgaria for 35 years until the collapse of his hardline communist regime in 1989, was charged in 1992 with discrimination for forcing ethnic Turks to change their Islamic names for Bulgarian ones in the 1980s and with curbing their religious and cultural practices.
That case has never come to court.
Between January 1995 and November 1996, 744 premeditated murders were committed in this small Balkan country and 4,391 cars were stolen, interior ministry figures show.
In 1996 the number of prisoners increased by 2,800 against 1995, officials said.

"All 12 prisons and 28 detention centres are congested and we are opening new detention centres. Last year we opened three new centres," Traikov said, adding that a project for a new jail was gathering dust on the shelf due to lack of money.
